Portrait

The story so far.

I grew up in Cameroon watching clinics lose patient records to handwriting errors and hospitals fail basic queue management. These were not funding problems. They were data problems. That distinction shaped everything that came after.

At 15, from thousands of candidates across Cameroon, only 9 students were selected for the U.S. Department of State's Kennedy-Lugar YES Program. I was one of them. The American school placed me directly in Grade 12, two full years ahead. I graduated Magna Cum Laude, GPA 3.583, in a foreign language, an entirely different educational system, while competing in varsity cross-country and logging over 100 certified community service hours.

Throughout every single year of secondary school, I was elected class delegate (chef de classe) by my peers. Managing conflicts, mediating between students and faculty, carrying collective responsibility while maintaining top academic performance. Leadership earned through trust, not appointment.

Back home, I channelled that international perspective into community work: first-aid training for 60 youth across three cities, fundraising for school supplies, girls' skills workshops, school infrastructure improvement. Every initiative reinforced the same conviction: systems and data determine outcomes more than funding does.

"I did not wait for a university lab to begin asking the important questions. The hospital waiting rooms of Cameroon were my first research environment."

Featured Project

Innovation Built from Observation

Healthcare · Data Engineering · Cameroon
MbaoMed

A digital patient registration prototype targeting two critical failures observed firsthand in Cameroonian hospitals: catastrophic data loss from handwritten records, and unmanageable queue times that cost people hours — sometimes care itself.

MbaoMed was not assigned by a syllabus. It emerged from years of direct observation: clinic visits, community health work, conversations with patients and staff, all converging on a single diagnostic question: why do functioning hospitals keep losing patients to data chaos?

Conceptualized with a research-first methodology and built with available tools including AI assistance for rapid prototyping, while maintaining full conceptual ownership and engineering direction.

PythonC++Data EngineeringAlgorithm DesignHealthcare ITOOP
The Problem
Cameroonian clinics lose patient records to handwriting errors daily. Queue management fails because there is no data layer beneath it. These are engineering problems wearing the disguise of funding problems.
See community context → Instagram
The Insight
Six community service projects across three cities gave direct access to how institutions fail their people. The gap between the systems I encountered in the United States and those I returned to in Cameroon is real — and it is bridgeable.
The Approach
Empirical before technical. Patient observation, workflow mapping, and stakeholder input before a single line of code. AI-assisted rapid prototyping to compress the gap between insight and functional prototype.
What Comes Next
A research paper documenting the methodology is in preparation. The goal: a replicable model for building functional health data infrastructure with limited resources, AI assistance, and empirical community grounding.
